It Was Already Dobbs: Abortion Bans and Maternal Health
After Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization, physicians and medical societies warned that state abortion bans would spill over into care for miscarriage, ectopic pregnancy, and terminations for the health of the mother or fetus, harming pregnant women well beyond elective abortion. I test that prediction with a novel pregnancy-level dataset built from claims for nearly 1 million continuously insured pregnancies conceived between 2020 and 2024, comparing 15 ban states with 25 protected jurisdictions in a stacked difference-in-differences design. The bans had limited effects on maternal health: confidence intervals rule out increases in hypertensive disorders above 5.1 percent and in severe maternal morbidity above 15.8 percent, and the timing and intensity of care changed little. Births rose only slightly, and the women who became pregnant after the bans were no less healthy than those before. Insured abortion was already rare in ban states before the bans, at about 1 percent of pregnancy endings, suggesting that formalizing an already restricted environment changed little.
Scheduled Presentation: SEA 2026


First Do No Harm: The Labor Market Consequences of a Physician Disciplinary Record
with Colleen Carey and Amanda Agan
Using a novel dataset of 70,000 state medical board disciplinary actions across more than 40 states (2008–2023), we provide the first evidence on how State Medical Board discipline affects subsequent physician careers. Most disciplined physicians continue practicing—often in a new state and supplying fewer claims—evidence that can inform the optimal design of state oversight and disciplinary actions.
Presented at APPAM 2025 Presented at SOLE 2026 Presented at ASHE 2026 Scheduled Presentation: SEA 2026


Born After Dobbs: Abortion Bans, Prenatal Diagnosis, and the Prevalence of Congenital Conditions
Abortion bans may change which pregnancies continue after a serious prenatal diagnosis. I test whether bans raised the prevalence at birth of conditions usually detected during pregnancy, such as Down syndrome, relative to conditions that cannot be detected before birth, and follow affected infants through their first year of care.


Hard to Concentrate: Prenatal Air Pollution and Childhood ADHD
Using medical claims for millions of children and Clean Air Act nonattainment designations that required states to reduce fine particulate pollution, I study whether exposure before birth raises the probability of an ADHD diagnosis later in childhood. Preliminary evidence shows that higher county air pollution is associated with more visits for ADHD, anxiety, and depression among children in the same year.

title: Gabrielle Sorresso
text:
Gabrielle Sorresso
PhD Candidate, Cornell Jeb E. Brooks School of Public Policy


Hi, I’m Gabrielle — a 5th-year PhD candidate at the Cornell Jeb E. Brooks School of Public Policy. I’m an applied microeconomist studying maternal, infant, and family health. I use causal inference methods and large-scale administrative data, primarily healthcare claims. The core of my current research agenda is how health and reproductive policy affects women before, during, and after pregnancy, as well as the health of their children. I pay particular attention to how these effects differ by insurance coverage, race and ethnicity, and place.
My current work examines the Dobbs decision: how state abortion bans affected maternal health and changed who becomes pregnant, and whether they changed the prevalence of congenital conditions among infants born after the bans. This work was recognized with the Horowitz Foundation’s Most Outstanding Project Award. To answer these questions, I built a pregnancy-level dataset from raw insurance claims that follows women from the year before conception through the year after birth. I also have joint work with Colleen Carey and Amanda Agan on how state medical board discipline shapes physicians’ careers and provision of care, and with Sharon Sassler on gender wage gaps and spousal occupation.
I am affiliated with the Cornell Population Center and the Cornell Health Policy Center.
